subtype: Approach: assuming it will never happen [Pitfall]
passage: "Boring," said Yogesh when Papa unrolled the fire-drill card on the sofa. "Fires only happen to strangers." He rolled his eyes and went back to his game. Three weeks later, in the kitchen, the burner flame jumped to the curtain. Yogesh stood with a glass in his hand, staring. Which door? Which way? What was step one? The steps he had laughed at were nowhere in his head. "Out! Now!" His father Jagdish grabbed his arm, pulled him into the corridor and shut the door, while Mummy shouted for the neighbours and rang the fire brigade. Downstairs, Yogesh's knees shook. He had stood still for far too long.

qa.q: Who pulled Yogesh out of the kitchen?
qa.a: His father Jagdish pulled him out.

qa.q: What was Yogesh feeling as he stood in the kitchen with the glass?
qa.a: Frozen and scared, and confused, since none of the steps he had laughed at came to mind.

qa.q: What would you advise Yogesh to do now, and why?
qa.a: Yogesh could ask to practise the drill again and take it seriously, because knowing the steps lets his body move when he is frightened.

qa.q: What might Jagdish be feeling as he pulls Yogesh into the corridor?
qa.a: Jagdish is likely frightened and urgent, wanting only to get his son out, and probably relieved once they are outside.

grounding: A boy dismisses fire drills as boring, so when the kitchen catches fire he hesitates and cannot remember the steps.
